Statistical analysis will be undertaken to ascertain any relationships between the Health of the Nation Outcome Scales 12-question assessment tool (HoNOS) and/or cluster data and patient prognosis as held within the Mental Health & Learning Disabilities Data Set (MHLDDS). The HoNOS is an outcome measure that is used in an adapted form as the Mental Health Clustering tool in order to identify patient need and facilitate their classification. The MHLDDS data will not be linked to any other data source. 
By adding the years of life lost to premature mortality (YLL) to the years lived with disability (YLDs) the Royal College of Psychiatrists (RCPsych) quote figures of 22.8% of the UK’s Disability adjusted life years (DALYs) being caused by mental illness, affecting 11 million people (Royal College of Psychiatrists, 2010). The human cost (e.g. in terms of distress specifically caused by psychotic experiences such as those allocated to cluster 10) varies widely between individuals. Some people are untroubled and continue to lead productive and fulfilling lives whilst others struggle to cope, become very distressed and require the support of specialist mental health services to maintain their safety and (in the minority of cases the safety of others) (Cooke, 2014). 
In terms of financial costs, benchmarking tables are produced by the Department of Health on an annual basis (Department of Health, 2014). These “Reference Costs” are calculated from financial submissions made by all statutory health providers. For mental health providers they show the average cost of community treatment and inpatient care for each cluster. By combining the most recently available national average costs (Department of Health, 2014) with the most recently available information from the Health and Social Care Information Centre (HSCIC, 2014) on the number of mental health treatment days delivered nationally by cluster (i.e. for the month of June 2015) it is clear that people experiencing psychosis (i.e. clusters 10-17) use a disproportionate amount of mental health resources. 
The mean cost of inpatient care is approximately 25 times that of community treatment (£222/day Vs £9/day) and 4.8% of psychosis treatment is undertaken in hospital (versus 1.4% for non-psychosis clusters and 1.0% for organic clusters). This differential is compounded by the increased costs of bed days for psychotic patients (in part due to increased staffing levels and the physical security of environment). Overall therefore whilst 28.2% of all treatment days are devoted to psychosis care, this patient group accounts for 60.6% of bed days. This results in them consuming: 39.0% of community costs; 69.6% of inpatient costs and 51.1% of total costs. Long before national costs were routinely presented by cluster, the Department of Health produced a Policy Implementation Guideline which required all English health economies to create Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) teams with a specific remit to proactively case-find and intensively treat patients between the ages of 14-35 experiencing their first episode of psychosis (now described by cluster 10). They argued that there was evidence to suggest that intensive early intervention utilising evidence based treatments could significantly improve patient’s long term prognosis (Department of Health, 2001). The most recent summary of evidence-based treatment for psychosis published by the National Institute of Clinical Excellence( NICE) finds Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Family Interventions (FI) to be the most cost-effective treatments for psychosis saving £989 and £2,634 per patient respectively (NICE, 2014). Whilst these treatments are not appropriate for all psychotic patients, EIP teams (which routinely deliver these interventions to psychotic patients in cluster 10) have been found to be cost-effective when compared to standard community psychiatric treatment with reductions in bed-usage the most significant saving (NICE, 2014). Despite this, hospital admissions still occur in cluster 10 (3.3% of treatment days according to table 4) and some EIP services find a few (10%) heavy bed-users significantly skew their overall admission rates (Dodgson, Ross, Tiffin, Mitford, & Brabban, 2012). It is unclear whether this sub-set of patients have simply reached their functional “glass ceiling” (Carter, 2006) or whether they could achieve better outcomes given the right circumstances. It is therefore possible that there may be a small cohort of expensive patients who could benefit from modifications to standard EIP treatment to optimise outcomes. This is clearly one reason why further research is strongly advocated for this area (NICE, 2014). Clearly, in addition to developing and testing modifications to treatments it will also be helpful to establish clinically meaningful ways of proactively identifying the sub-set of patients for whom they may be beneficial and hence cost-effective. The broad aim of this research is therefore to investigate whether the Mental Health PbR dataset can be used to predict poor prognosis in patients experiencing their first episode of psychosis.
NB. The reason for requesting Mental Health Act data is that this is an important and well established factor in defining patient outcomes. Without this information the analysis would have far less clinical utility as the only variables that could be used to indicate prognosis would be psychiatric bed days and psychiatric admissions.
The named individual is the applicant but is using resources from within Northumberland Tyne and Wear NHS FT to ensure IG requirements are met. Sheffield University’s involvement is purely to provide academic supervision and guidance but at no time will they have access to the data extract, merely the aggregated, non-disclosive results with small number suppression.

Processing Activities• Data will be received by The Trust’s Informatics Department via secure means • The data will be stored at all times on Trust secured file servers and accessed via (but not stored on) an encrypted laptop. • The MHLDDS data will be processed by the Trust’s Informatics Department to produce extract tables to facilitate data analysis in analytical tools including SPSS and Excel (no data linkage will take place) • The data will be analysed for the purpose outlined in the application by the applicant and high level statistical output will be produced. • Following the production of statistical reports, dissertation and publications, the data will be retained on secure Trust equipment until the above retention period is reached. NB. The data will be stored at all times on secured NHS Trust servers, with access limited to individuals directly employed by the Trust. When being processed using SPSS, the data will be accessed via (but not stored on) a Trust encrypted and password protected laptop. Servers and laptops all comply with relevant Data Protection standards as per section 7.

Expected OutputOutput 1: Initially an MSc dissertation for Sheffield University will be produced by end of 2016 on the work undertaken. Output 2: A report explaining the results and how they may be applied in practice (see: “Interpretation of CROM Outcomes-general guidance for commissioners and providers” at: http://www.cppconsortium.nhs.uk/crom.php for an example) will also be made available to NHS England’s Pricing team in Quarter 3 of 2015/16 (whose mental health lead is again supportive of the work) for dissemination to all Mental Health trusts and via the Early Intervention in Psychosis Networks that exist within the NHS. Additionally the report will be posted on the consortium’s website (which has become a useful repository for clustering work) and emailed to each Trust’s project lead for circulation to clinicians within all Mental Health trusts in Yorkshire and Humber and the North East areas. Output 3: Finally attempts will be made to publish all clinically useful results in appropriate peer reviewed journals. All of the above publications will be limited to summarised results (aggregate, non-disclosive results with small numbers suppressed) rather than elements of the original extract and will clearly acknowledge the source of the data used. Information from this analysis will be produced in line with the published MHMDS/MHLDDS suppression rules, which can be found here: http://www.hscic.gov.uk/media/14272/Monthly-MHMDS-Reports---2014-15-Methodological-change/pdf/MHMDS_Reports_-_Methodological_Change.pdf

Expected Measurable BenefitsAny clinically useful correlations between HoNOS and/or cluster data and patient prognosis will be considered for local use. To do so, the statistical relationships determined from this analysis of MHMDS data will be used to produce guidance of how to interpret the existing national algorithm results and/or a set of revised algorithms. When local patient HoNOS ratings are entered into the local Electronic Patient Record system by the EIP healthcare professional, the intention is to ensure any patients likely to be poor responders are automatically flagged to staff at the point they enter the data thus allowing them to take a more assertive/revised approach to their treatment. The results will also be publicised within the NHS as described above to allow community psychiatric teams to more promptly identify patients who are likely to require a different / more intensive approach to their treatment from the outset of their care. Given the report, it will be possible for organisations and individuals to identify these patients using the excel-based algorithms which have already been provided to them by the consortium and NHS England. Given the severe impact of psychosis on quality of life described earlier in this application it is clear that this type of research (which has been advocated by NICE in 2014) has the potential to significantly impact on early identification and hence improved treatment of the 10% of poor responders to standard EIP treatment. According to the recent NHS Early Intervention In Psychosis Commissioning Guide, effective early treatment can improve: • prognosis, • the likelihood of recovery and • the leading of full, hopeful and productive lives. As a result even a modest improvement in the efficacy of their care could have a significant impact on these factors and hence the overall quality of care provided. From a financial perspective, using the estimates provided earlier, at a local level given the Trust’s caseload of cluster 10s (approx. 500 at any one time) up to £181,150 could be saved recurrently on the 10% of patients going onto make very high use of the Trusts psychiatric beds if early identification allows treatment to be altered in order to deliver the financial benefits that Early intervention yields for the other 90%. Clearly if this figure is factored up to include all EIP teams this figure becomes a significant potential saving. Overall therefore, the patient benefits of this research are anticipated to include: • Earlier identification of treatment resistant patients • Improved outcomes for these treatment resistant patients in terms of: o Reduced hospital admissions o Reduced detentions under the Mental Health Act o Increased likelihood of symptom remission o Increased likelihood of employment o Improved quality of life o Improved satisfaction with mental health services And the service benefits are anticipated to include: • A more effective way of targeting resources • Reduced demand on psychiatric beds • Reduced use of the Mental Health Act (and its associated costs) • Cost reductions as outlined earlier
